meta.title: TCNJ NASA Human Lander Challenge
meta.description: TCNJ's NASA Human Lander Challenge capstone project: the project and the team, past and present.

home.lede: NASA's Human Lander Challenge is asking teams to solve problems in lunar surface communications equipment, a challenge that leans electrical engineering. The College of New Jersey's team is tackling it from a mechanical angle instead. We're designing a dust-tolerant connector for the base of a lunar antenna: the mechanical joint where regolith works its way in, jams the hardware, and takes the signal with it.
home.panel_hulc_body: NASA's Human Lander Challenge is a national university design competition run with the National Institute of Aerospace, aimed at the technology NASA needs for its Artemis campaign to return humans to the Moon. Each year NASA opens a new focus area for teams to design against. This cycle (labeled "2027") centers on lunar surface communications equipment. Teams submit proposals, then present forward-phase designs to NASA reviewers.

project.artemis_body: NASA's Artemis campaign is the agency's push to return astronauts to the Moon and build a sustainable presence there ahead of eventual Mars missions. Artemis II carried a crew around the Moon and back in April 2026, the first crewed lunar flight in over fifty years. Artemis III follows in 2027 as an orbital checkout flight, with the first crewed landing now planned for Artemis IV in 2028.
project.angle_body_1: This year's HuLC theme (the "2027" cycle) centers on lunar surface communications equipment, an area that leans electrical engineering. Our team is approaching it from a mechanical lens instead, and we've narrowed our focus to the connector at the base of a lunar antenna.
project.angle_body_2: Lunar regolith is sharp and electrostatically charged. It works into the clearances of mechanical joints, raises friction, and eventually jams them, a failure mode documented repeatedly across the Apollo missions, where lubricating the mechanisms between EVAs wasn't enough to keep them moving. NASA currently lists dust-tolerant rotary joints as an open technology gap. Our connector is designed to seal against that intrusion while still allowing a few degrees of rotation for fine pointing adjustment, since a directional antenna only delivers its gain if it stays aimed. Focusing on one component, rather than redesigning an entire antenna system, also gives us something we can realistically simulate, manufacture, and test with the vacuum chamber and other resources available at TCNJ.

phases.title: Scoping
phases.body: Reviewed NASA's HuLC archives, the lunar dust mitigation literature, and our program's past two years of projects to scope the problem.

phases.title: Design Research
phases.body: Building the connector design from the ground up: contact physics, space-rated connector standards, and NASA's dust-tolerant mechanism work.

phases.title: Proposal
phases.body: Proposal package and concept video submitted to NASA / NIA. Due March 4, 2027.

phases.title: HuLC Forum
phases.body: Finalist teams present to NASA reviewers in Huntsville, Alabama. June 21–24, 2027.
